modules.title: Name the whole
modules.desc: Identify what one whole stands for, then find a fractional share of it.
modules.rule: A fraction is a share of a named whole: split into equal parts, take the top-number of them.
teach: Always start by naming the whole: '1 (the whole) is all 30 marbles / 40 children / 60 pages'.
The bottom number cuts the whole into equal parts; the top number counts how many you take.
part = (top/bottom) x whole.
contrast: Same share, different whole, different amount.
modules.transfer: Write two stories where 1/4 of the whole is 10. What must the whole be in each?

modules.title: Part & complement from a figure
modules.desc: Read a shaded figure: name the whole, the shaded part, and the plain complement.
modules.rule: In a figure the bottom number is the count of equal parts; shaded + plain = 1.
teach: Count every equal part to get the bottom number.
Count the shaded parts to get the top number.
The complement is the whole minus the shaded part.
modules.transfer: Shade a strip so the plain part is 2/5. How many of 5 parts stay shaded?

modules.title: Equivalent fractions & odd-one-out
modules.desc: Build equal fractions by scaling both numbers, and spot the fraction that does not belong.
modules.rule: Multiply or divide top and bottom by the SAME number to keep the share equal.
teach: Scaling both numbers by the same factor does not change the share.
To test if fractions are equal, reduce each to lowest terms.
The odd one out reduces to a different lowest-terms fraction.
contrast: 8/16 = 1/2, which is the stranger among thirds.
modules.transfer: Write three fractions equal to 3/4, then one that only looks similar but isn't.

modules.title: Lowest terms via GCD
modules.desc: Simplify a fraction by dividing top and bottom by their greatest common factor.
modules.rule: Lowest terms: divide out the GCF until top and bottom share no factor above 1.
teach: Find the greatest common factor of the top and bottom.
Divide BOTH by it in one clean step.
Stop when the only shared factor is 1.
contrast: Dividing only by 2 would leave 9/12, not finished.
modules.transfer: Simplify 20/50 two ways: dividing by 2 then 5, or by 10 at once.

modules.title: Compare & order fractions
modules.desc: Compare fractions by matching denominators; beware 'bigger bottom = bigger'.
modules.rule: Give a common bottom, then the bigger top wins.
teach: Unlike bottoms mean unlike part-sizes — match them first.
A bigger bottom means SMALLER parts, not a bigger fraction.
With equal bottoms, compare the tops.
contrast: The bigger bottom is the smaller share.
modules.transfer: Order 2/3, 3/4, 5/6 from smallest to largest using bottom 12.

modules.title: Add & subtract like fractions
modules.desc: Combine fractions that already share a bottom by working only on the tops.
modules.rule: Same bottom: add or subtract the tops, keep the bottom, then simplify.
teach: Equal bottoms mean equal-size parts you can count together.
Combine the tops; the bottom never changes.
Simplify the result to lowest terms.
contrast: Writing 5/10 would wrongly add the bottoms.
modules.transfer: Find two eighths that add to exactly 1.

modules.title: Add & subtract unlike fractions
modules.desc: Combine fractions with different bottoms by first finding the least common denominator.
modules.rule: Unlike bottoms: rewrite over the LCD, then combine the tops.
teach: Different bottoms must be matched before combining.
Use the least common multiple of the bottoms as the LCD.
Never add tops and bottoms separately.
contrast: 2/5 is NOT the answer — that adds tops and bottoms.
modules.transfer: Add 1/4 + 1/6 by first finding the LCD of 4 and 6.

modules.title: Mixed and improper fractions
modules.desc: Convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions and add mixed numbers.
modules.rule: Improper top = whole x bottom + part-top; mixed = whole groups + leftover.
teach: Mixed to improper: wholes x bottom, add the part-top, keep the bottom.
Improper to mixed: divide top by bottom for the whole, remainder over the bottom.
Add mixed numbers by matching fraction bottoms, then combining wholes and parts.
contrast: 11/4 = 2 3/4, since 4 goes into 11 twice with 3 left.
modules.transfer: Turn 17/5 into a mixed number, then back again.

modules.title: Fraction of a quantity, multiply & divide
modules.desc: Use 'of' = multiply, multiply fractions straight across, and divide by flipping.
modules.rule: 'of' and 'x' both multiply; to divide, multiply by the reciprocal.
teach: 'A fraction OF an amount' means fraction x amount.
Multiply fractions: tops x tops over bottoms x bottoms.
Divide fractions: flip the divisor and multiply.
modules.transfer: Work out 1/2 of 3/4 two ways: as 'of' and as multiply.

modules.title: Averages, series & fraction equations
modules.desc: Average fractions, find the nth term of a fraction series, and solve Q-over-number equations.
modules.rule: Average = sum / count; a series hides a steady pattern; clear fractions to solve for Q.
teach: Average of fractions: add them, then divide by how many there are.
A fraction series becomes clear once every term shares one bottom.
Solve fraction equations by multiplying every term by the common bottom.
modules.transfer: Solve Q/4 + Q/6 = Q/12 + 15 by clearing with bottom 12.

questions.title: Priya's marbles
questions.story: Priya has 30 marbles. She gives 1/3 of them to a friend. How many marbles does she give away?

stages.prompt: What amount stands for the whole (everything we start with)?
stages.hint: Complete: the whole is all marbles we begin with.

options.feedback: Yes — the whole is every one of the 30 marbles we start with.
That is the share we act on, not the whole we measure it against.

options.text: The number 1 because it is on top of the fraction
options.feedback: The top number counts parts of the share — it is not the size of the whole.

stages.prompt: What does 1/3 of the whole mean here?
stages.hint: A fraction cuts the whole into equal parts; the top number counts how many.

options.text: Cut 30 into 3 equal parts, then take 1
options.feedback: Right — split into 3 equal groups and keep 1 of them.
A fraction is not subtraction — it splits into equal parts first.
The two numbers of a fraction are a part-count and a part-size, not amounts to add on.

stages.prompt: Which calculation finds 1/3 of 30?
stages.hint: part = (fraction) x whole.

options.feedback: Exactly — (1/3) x 30 = 10 marbles.
That subtracts the bottom number as if it were an amount in the story.
Dividing only by the top number ignores how many parts we keep.

worked: The whole is all 30 marbles in her bag.
1/3 means split 30 into 3 equal parts, then take 1.
questions.check: The two shares add back to the whole: 10 + 20 = 30.
questions.explain: Name the whole first, then the share. The whole is what 'the whole fraction' (1) stands for.
